title: Art and audio
thesis: In a roguelike, presentation is a budget and a language before it is decoration: the same few glyphs, tiles, sounds and loops are seen and heard thousands of times, so they must be cheap to make, quick to read and slow to wear out. Abstraction (ASCII, strong tile forms, symbolic sound) lets players imagine and lets designers afford huge content; when you move beyond it, kitbash and generate within one coherent style, add juice that fits the tone, and design music and sound for repetition and an unknown order of play.

sections.heading: ASCII or graphics: what the choice costs and buys
sections.brief: Open the chapter with the decision every roguelike faces first. Lead with the convergence between Santiago Zapata and Evan Ovadia: character display makes a new monster cost a glyph, a colour, a description and data, which is what lets roguelikes afford huge casts and complex interactions; add Ovadia's reusability point (a green o is an orc, a purple o a chieftain), Josh Ge on ASCII making content easy, JP LeBreton on ASCII discretising visual decisions for a solo artist, and Rich Wilson on how Dwarf Fortress depicts sitting as two overlapping glyphs where AAA needs nav meshes and animation. Then stage the counter-argument: Zapata (mediocre graphics please no one; half-measure sprites satisfy nobody, go all the way or stay with characters) and Thomas Biskup (mainstream needs graphics; Ultimate ADOM's focus) converge that graphics are about audience, and Biskup's crowdfunding talk shows the cost (art took three and a half to four of five years) and the 2.5D choice. Add Josh Ge's animated UI as a cheap middle path, Alphaman's coloured ASCII as history, and Zeno Rogue on why pixel art fails in hyperbolic space as a case where the geometry decides. End with guidance: decide by audience and content volume, budget the full cost of graphics honestly, and don't ship a half-measure.

sections.heading: What abstraction does for the player
sections.brief: Argue why abstract representation is a feature, not a fallback. droqen (the @ boils away everything that doesn't matter; low-res pixel art works the same way) and Jamie Brittain (low fidelity cues players to co-create the space) converge; set Evan Ovadia against them as the nuance: ASCII does not automatically evoke imagination, it needs just enough extra detail (flickering floor colours), and he calls the secret an open question, also noting other ASCII/sprite hybrids remain to be found. Add Alexandra Leonhart's 'glyph kinship' between the @ and the monsters. Then move to borrowed meaning: Cara Esten Hurtle (old-software constraints breed creativity, but use retro aesthetics only when the old medium tells a story nothing else could), G blekkenhorst (retro interface styles set expectations and date artefacts in the fiction), Chogue's Unicode chess pieces and CGA palette evoking Rogue, Dwarf Fortress reusing ADOM's quote-mark grass and Rogue's smiley. Close with presentation as meaning: Joseph Hewitt's magician point that presentation matters as much as mechanism, and Darren Grey's two Rogue box-art covers that promise different games. Guidance: choose representation for what it lets the player imagine and what it signals, and add only the detail that triggers imagination.

sections.heading: The craft of text art
sections.brief: A practical section on drawing, colouring and animating with characters, specific enough to work from. Start with the data model (JP LeBreton: a grid of cells, each a character index plus foreground and background palette indices) and his point that the choice of character set and palette has a massive effect on the result; then Gabriel Santos's three styles (block, line, box drawing) and Gabriel's lightning-talk case for ASCII art as an art form (Stone Story). Work through Santos's techniques: avoid letters and digits inside art (the eye reads them as text), Unicode only where it keeps the style, glyph swaps that change lighting, anti-aliasing near-vertical lines, consistent glyph treatments as a material language, negative space to separate overlapping shapes, accidental shadows on patterned floors, and fast iteration once glyph combos are memorised. Then colour and effects within the grid: Jeremiah Reid's desaturated palette as the cheapest upgrade and his point that Brogue and Cogmind look striking on-grid, Cogmind's 9x9 hidden particle subgrid, and Santos's deliberately simple particle emitter. End with animation: layered scenes, the same pre-production process as other animation (test size in context first), and subtractive build-up animation. Guidance should be a short list of rules of thumb.

sections.heading: Tiles that read like glyphs
sections.brief: How to make tiles as legible as ASCII. Lead with Joel Ryan's 'major forms' (a few solid areas and lines so experienced players read tiles almost like symbols, versus pixel-noisy mud), and set it beside Josh Ge's Cogmind tiles (monochrome, identifiable by shape, offered because 66 of 84 sampled players use tiles): two independent tile designers converging on keeping ASCII's qualities. Then Ryan's toolkit from Sil-Q: borrow ASCII's strengths (diamond player, M-shaped spider), silhouettes that classify an unseen monster, reserving pixel size to signal threat, contrasting detail frequency between tiles and background, colour coding abilities, a tileset-wide outline decided from day one, a forced 256-colour shared palette that improved coherence, and drawing what serves the game and its lore rather than what you want to draw. Add Sea Of Rifts' exaggerated proportions for readability from a distant camera. Close with Ryan's legacy-code cases (broken NPP Angband tile mapping, 89 weapon combinations squeezed into 16 tiles) as cautions about scope. Guidance: a checklist of readability rules for tile artists.

sections.heading: Creatures whose look says what they do
sections.brief: Argue that monster art is UX and that roguelikes need many monsters. Open with Subset Games (Justin Ma and Matthew Davis): design creatures backwards from mechanics so the visual telegraphs function (rock race for high health, mantis for stabbing), with the mosquito-turned-squid as a warning about placeholder names; pair with Marlowe Dobbe deriving an enemy's look from its spec (the sad cauldron creature) and her argument that replayability demands a large, distinct cast. Then extend 'look shows state' to simulations and non-violent games: Liza Knipscher's Bioloom aims to show the clearest picture of simulation data (age by per-part scaling, death by shrinking skin to bones) and Tabea Iseli's Grimoire Groves uses plant growth stages so players read spells as helping, not hurting. Finish with Dobbe's process for generating many concepts: the list of 10, reference as legitimate (many sources, take parts, never trace), what to extract from reference, a personal reference library, the live 'castle bruiser' combination, and mood boards for art direction; Hintline 93's photographed emotion poses as another way to produce many expressive variants. Guidance: spec mechanics first, then pick visuals that teach them; generate concepts by combining references.

sections.heading: Art on a budget: borrow, kitbash, keep it coherent
sections.brief: The small-team art problem. Lead with convergence on kitbashing: Sergio Garces (procedural 3D environments from pre-made pieces like LEGO rather than noise and fractals), Max Bottega (3-4 small asset sets per biome smashed into all its props), and Phillip Daigle (kit-bash nearly-right open-licensed art into something bespoke; Wyrmsun's layered sprites for Rogue's Gate). Add Sofie Kjær Schmidt's Sea Of Rifts goal of most variation from fewest assets, and Evan Ovadia's symbolic graphics (trace icons in a font editor, render as outlined meshes) as the non-artist's route. Then the central warning, where several talks converge: coherence. Garces (asset flips fail; match colour, polygon density and style; replace materials), Ovadia (mixing sprite sheets clashes), and Schmidt (bought assets lack source files and risk looking like stock photos; unify with post-processing); set Garces's 'store assets are like casting an actor' legitimacy argument beside Schmidt's wariness. End with procedural generation of presentation itself: Thomas Robertson's procedural super attacks, and Courtney Liessen on how unbounded multipliers break the assumption that effects come in fixed tiers. Guidance: pick one style and source, kitbash within it, and plan for effects that scale.

sections.heading: Making generated spaces look art-directed
sections.brief: Generated environments tend to look random (Max Bottega's framing problem); this section collects the art-side fixes. Bottega's 'uniform variation' (one or two hero props per tile among generic props), props 'on their own feet' with ground bases and clustered debris, self-contained walls, and a composite camera for keeping biome colours compatible; Loren Schmidt's spatial frequency distribution (mix large gestural forms with fine detail so the eye can rest) converges with Bottega's point about attention. Then procedural dressing over hand-made structure: deepnight's Dead Cells decorator and LDtk rule-based auto-tiling. Then shader-driven variety from Sea Of Rifts (Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt): HSV colour swaps from three atlases that also signal faction, a per-object hash of height and rotation for free tint variation (two talks describe it; present once, cite both), sub-tiling trim sheets, and their claim that shaders are under-explored in procedural games. End with Sergio Garces's warning that generated 3D layouts can't use baked lighting, so plan dynamic lighting early. Guidance: let the generator place, let art rules compose.

sections.heading: Juice: making turns feel alive
sections.brief: Start part 2 with game feel. Define juice with Chris McCormick (sound and animation in response to input that make a game feel alive) and Jeremiah Reid (maximum output for minimum input; can be mechanical too), then Reid's key claim that juice is 'coded in, not drawn in' (tweens of scale, position, rotation, colour) so a solo programmer can do it, and his regret at not juicing Golden Krone Hotel earlier. Give the technique kit specific enough to implement: linear and exponential easing (shave a fixed percent of the delta), squash and stretch with a parabolic hop, anticipation lean and delay, per-step move queues and a lagging camera, directional screen shake, hit flashes and damage numbers with bigger crits, leaving corpses. Show layering via Fidel Dungeon Rescue and the Chicken Sword demo, juicy mechanics (Jupiter Hell's shell-by-shell reload), and browser implementation (McCormick's divs over rot.js, CSS animations in Smallest Quest, Asteroid). Then stage the limits: Reid on matching tone (Infra Arcana would not want bounce; Teleglitch too much), Tabea Iseli finding almost half of the screenshake canon is about violence and replacing it with laughing, cheering plants, and McCormick hoping depth and juice need not trade off. Close with Adrian Zeyfang's NecroDancer rollback animation identities as an edge case. Guidance: add juice early, keep it to the game's tone, and never let it block input.

sections.heading: Sound design for games that are mostly symbols
sections.brief: Argue that sound, including silence, is design. Lead with Julian K. Jarboe (roguelike developers already understand that abstract symbols convey a lot, so they are suited to sound) and Josh Ge (sound supports imagination of an ASCII world without hijacking it; Cogmind's 1,000+ samples and positional ambient machines you hear around corners). Then Jarboe's process: atmosphere beyond music and effects, why players listen and that some will mute, genre as a promise and the sonic-association worksheet, feel-accurate foley (celery for a punch), collage and free assets as legitimate, audio sprites, mixing on good headphones with consistent volume over quality, and MIDI's public-domain value. Then meaning in feedback sounds: Xalavier Nelson Jr. on the moral weight of a quest-complete sound in Space Warlord Organ Trading Simulator. Then voice: Neutrinowatch moving from spliced recordings to text-to-speech and translating DAW operations into code, set beside Paul Dean's warning that recorded voice can't be chopped procedurally (they agree). End with Synchrony's per-turn sound tracking under rollback so undone events don't play. Guidance: design the soundscape deliberately, start small with reusable libraries, and make every feedback sound say what you mean.

sections.heading: Music that survives a thousand runs
sections.brief: Roguelike music is heard over and over; this section is about avoiding ear fatigue. Lead with Crashtroid's definition of ear fatigue and his three remedies: segment loops so the player feels progress (Binding of Isaac's 'Repentant', Peglin's subtler changes), pace music to moment-to-moment play rather than just aesthetic (Roboquest's BPM matching fire rates versus Risk of Rain 2's exploratory score), and avoid jarring cuts with ambient/combat variants and shared motifs; then his flowchart reading of Hades' stingers and silences as quiet progress markers, and his 15-minute listening test. Converge with Jon Perry on Mini and Max using distinct music to signpost handcrafted areas, and Martin Pichlmair on Zelda's sequenced audio that can raise intensity by adding structure, trading off fullness. Add Santiago Zapata on background music for mood (DoomRL) and Phillip Daigle's warning not to bring a musician in while the game's direction still swings. Guidance: a short list of composition rules for replayed music.

sections.heading: Generative music: motifs, rhythms and the composer's hand
sections.brief: How to generate music rather than loop it. Lead with Paul Hembree's thesis that a single generative rule is never enough and the designer must act as composer, curating a stylistic subset and layering; then Euclidean rhythms as an efficient representation of syncopation, his simpler quantised-tuplet construction (multiply, divide, floor with a rounding point), smooth rotation by sweeping the rounding point, the warning that they lose charm above about 24 slots, ornament substitution systems, and generating thousands of candidates filtered by perceptual controls. Set Sonat Uzun's Tea Garden beside this as the motif approach: pools of looping motif strings per aspect, motifs as recipes given notes by scale and chord progression, special symbols, PICO-8 channel collisions as happy accidents, and mood via scale and silence; note the contrast that Uzun trusts randomness while Hembree insists on curation, and that both build for one game's style. Then Nifflas's playful device approach for Rhythm Doggo (sorting arpeggiator, railway and train-stop devices, bouncing reflector percussion, Monty Hall melodies). Frame with history: Pichlmair on musical dice games as controlled random composition. End with Hembree's point that tools should output editable material (MIDI) rather than replace a workflow. Guidance: pick a representation, curate its parameter space, layer, and keep humans in the loop.

sections.heading: Music bound to the world and the game state
sections.brief: When order of play is unknown, tie music to something the player moves through. Lead with Paul Hembree's problem statement (you can't compose a linear piece for an unknown succession of states) and his proposal to underscore traversal by subtle harmonic change. Walk through Rite of Tephra in implementable detail: pitch lattices as spatial models (square/cubic suit game coordinates), a cubic lattice of pitch nodes 36 m apart driving scale and light colour, a 52 m sphere hearing seven to eight nodes, a random choice of curated tilings per level, live remixing of per-pitch-class orchestral stems (and its costs), and phasing loops whose interaction makes melody; use Super Metroid's Norfair modulation as the analytical example of discovery built into tonality. Then other bindings of music to state: Nifflas's chaos node and named node groups that game code drives, and his placing songs through the level so the level, not the music engine, manages long-term intensity; Tyler Coleman on FFT and sonification (Mini Metro); Isaac Io Schankler's orb whose size and loudness pace breathing. Guidance: choose the game variable the music should follow, make the mapping musical rather than realistic, and calibrate it to player speed.

sections.heading: Pushing the medium
sections.brief: The chapter's frontier: what roguelike presentation has not yet tried. Lead with Nick Montfort's challenge to do with the computer display what Steve McCaffery did with the typewriter in Carnival, supported by concrete poetry (layout carries meaning), dirty concrete, Houédard's microspaced 3D forms, and his distinction between ASCII art that depicts and roguelikes that engage space. Then live examples of pushing: Todd Furmanski's Forska post-processing the same world as mosaic, oil painting or ASCII; Chelsea Thompto rendering Three.js scenes as ASCII to undercut realism; Greg L's 3 ms PICO-8 bloom by bit-packed convolution; Pokemon Glitch's reactive corruption; Ben Berman's ML animation from motion capture; bleeptrack taking generators into fabric prints and laser-cut paper, and Nat Alison's prime visualisations of local order and global chaos. Guidance: treat the display as a material to explore, not a solved problem, and note these are open directions rather than established practice.
